title: Contingency-Fee Meter Audits for Water Utilities
one_liner: Test the big commercial and industrial meters that under-register, replace them, and take a share of the new billed revenue for two years.
customer: Mid-size water and wastewater utilities (20k-500k connections) with large commercial bases, private regulated water companies, and utilities serving new large loads such as data centers and fabs. The utility pays from recovered revenue.
problem: Everyone sells AI leak detection, but in many audits apparent losses (meter under-registration, billing errors, unauthorized use) are comparable to real losses. Large compound meters under-register at low flow, and 1% of a data center's consumption is a lot of money. Utilities under rate pressure and drought-reduced volumes have no capex budget for meter programs.
solution: Prioritize the top 5% of accounts using billing anomalies (size versus consumption history). Field-test meters with a mobile test bench and clamp-on verification, then repair or replace. The company fronts the work and takes 20-35% of incremental revenue for 24 months. Software ranks accounts, and reports feed the AWWA-style utility audit.
why_now: Drought cuts volumes and rate pressure is intense. Private water companies invested about $6.8B in 2025 and must justify revenue. New industrial loads make each meter worth more.
revenue_model: 20-35% of incremental billed revenue for two years, with no upfront cost to the utility.
non_obvious_insight: Insiders chase leaks, which need capital and crews. Meter recovery is immediate cash with no capex approval, so it is easy to say yes to. Private and special-district utilities can sign contingency deals without a full municipal procurement.
first_30_days: Target three investor-owned utilities and two special districts. Offer a free desktop analysis of their top 200 commercial accounts using billing data. Test the ten most suspicious meters as a proof-of-value, and sign a contingency contract on the results.

title: Supply-Continuity Escrow for Hardware Startups
one_liner: Software-style source-code escrow, but for physical products: startups deposit CAD, BOMs and tooling data, and a pre-qualified micro-factory network is contractually obligated to keep making parts for buyers if the startup dies.
customer: Hardware startups selling to risk-averse institutional buyers (hospitals, cities, universities, fleet operators, utilities) who pay the fee, plus the buyers themselves as beneficiaries of an activation right.
problem: Procurement teams fear vendor death more than defects. A city buying 200 startup e-scooters or chargers, or a hospital buying a startup's carts or robots, has no continuity plan, so deals stall or die. When a hardware company collapses, its fleet is orphaned. The roughly 11,000 Fisker Ocean owners spent two years building their own parts supply chain through a nonprofit.
solution: A continuity package. Startups deposit CAD, drawings, BOM, supplier list, firmware build environment and key tooling data. We validate it by making trial 'trigger-ready' proof parts on printers, CNC and short-run PCB partners so that the plan is real and tested. A contract gives named buyers release rights on defined triggers (bankruptcy, 90 days with no shipments, end-of-life). Result: a one-page Continuity Letter the startup attaches to bids.
why_now: Hardware failures have piled up (Fisker, Canoo, Nikola and other consumer and mobility failures), so procurement officers have fresh horror stories. Low-cost printing, CNC and small-batch PCB fabrication now make it plausible to reproduce a wide range of parts locally without the original supply chain. Cities and health systems are buying more startup hardware in robotics, mobility and charging.
revenue_model: Annual escrow and validation fee from the vendor ($5k to $25k based on complexity), a paid proof-of-manufacturability audit, an activation fee (10% to 20% of fabricated-parts value) when triggered, and optional buyer-side monitoring of vendor health.
non_obvious_insight: It sells like insurance with a tiny loss ratio. The physical network is only activated a few percent of the time, but the deposit and the tested proof are what unlock enterprise deals for the startup. Because the startup pays to close a sale, the network is funded by growth spend rather than by rare disaster events. The hard part is proving manufacturability in advance, and that proof is the moat.
first_30_days: Talk to 10 hardware founders who are stuck in enterprise procurement and to 3 procurement or biomed managers who have been burned before. Offer a fixed-price $2,500 Continuity Letter (checklist audit plus one proof part) to the first five. Draft a simple template agreement with a startup-friendly law firm and line up two machine shops and a PCB house as network partners.

title: Medicaid Work-Rule Retention for Hospitals and Plans
one_liner: A text-first service that proves work hours and exemptions on behalf of Medicaid members, paid per retained member by the hospitals and health plans that would otherwise lose them.
customer: Safety-net hospitals, FQHC networks and Medicaid managed-care plans in expansion states. They pay roughly $4-12 per retained member per month or a fee per successful report.
problem: Under the 2025 budget law (OBBBA), expansion adults aged 19-64 must document about 80 hours a month of work, school or volunteering, or prove an exemption, with more frequent renewals. Deadlines start no later than January 1, 2027, with limited state extensions. Arkansas in 2018 showed that people mostly lost coverage from reporting failures, not from ineligibility. Members lose coverage over paperwork. Hospitals and plans then lose revenue and absorb uncompensated care.
solution: A retention layer that sits on the member side. It works over SMS and WhatsApp in multiple languages. It connects to the member's payroll, gig-platform earnings, school enrollment or caregiver records to auto-assemble monthly proof. It screens for the many exemptions (medically frail, parents of young children, substance-use treatment, recent release) and generates provider attestation letters from the clinic's own visit. It submits in each state's format, using portal automation and mail-in where needed. It nags before deadlines. A dashboard shows the plan or hospital which members are at risk before the coverage cliff. The same engine later covers SNAP work rules.
why_now: The law was signed in July 2025, and federal guidance and state build-outs are happening now for the 2027 start. Some states, such as Georgia with Pathways, already run work-reporting programs. The large incumbents (state-agency contractors) build for the state side, not for retention on the member side. Hospital CFOs are modeling large expansion-population losses this budget cycle. LLM agents plus computer-use can drive dozens of clunky state portals that never had APIs. Gig and payroll data connections make proof of hours automatic.
revenue_model: Per-member-per-month retention fee, or per-successful-report fee, paid by hospitals, FQHCs and plans. Later, state contracts and a SNAP work-requirement product on the same infrastructure.
non_obvious_insight: The payer is neither the patient nor the state. It is whoever loses revenue when a member drops. The failure is documentation friction, not eligibility. The cheapest evidence source is the member's own gig or payroll account plus the clinic visit itself, which can collect exemption proof for free.
first_30_days: Choose one state with an early or waiver-driven start and a large FQHC association. Meet revenue-cycle and financial-counseling leads at 5 FQHCs and hospitals. Publish a free state-by-state 'Am I exempt? Do my hours count?' checker to generate leads. Run a manual SMS concierge pilot with 200 members using a spreadsheet and volunteers, and measure on-time reporting rate. Convert the best result into a signed letter of intent for a per-retained-member fee.

title: Part-Time Retired Journeymen as Apprentice Supervisors
one_liner: Supervision-as-a-service: retired licensed tradespeople work 2-3 days a week as the supervising journeyman that lets small shops deploy the apprentices and helpers they already have.
customer: 5-25 employee electrical, plumbing and HVAC shops with unlicensed helpers or apprentices, starting in one state with clear ratio and qualifier rules. They pay by the hour.
problem: The headlines say the pipeline is the shortage, but the Gen Z enrollment surge is called a demographic mirage. For many shops the binding constraint is licensed supervision, because ratio rules cap helpers per journeyman. Data-center overtime ($130-170K for journeymen, vendor stat) pulls supervisors off residential work. ABC says most of the 349K 2026 shortfall is retirements, yet retirees hold exactly the scarce credential and are unused.
solution: A vetted, insured bench of retired journeymen and masters placed part-time in shops as supervising journeyman and mentor. The platform verifies licenses, runs employer-of-record or 1099 structure per state rules, handles workers' comp, and automates the apprenticeship hour logs boards require. Shops book blocks such as Tue-Thu 7-3.
why_now: ABC's 2026 gap of 349K is mostly retirement. Data centers now account for nearly a third of the shortage. Immigration enforcement removes helpers, so shops need to hire and supervise local apprentices fast. Trade-school hype is masking a thin pipeline.
revenue_model: Shops pay about $75-110 per hour billed. The platform keeps 20-25% and the retiree keeps the rest. Add $150-250 per month for hour-logging and compliance software.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce good is not labor, it is supervision minutes, and retirees want 16-hour weeks that no normal employer offers. A supervising journeyman unlocks one or two helpers billing at journeyman-adjacent rates, so shops can pay a premium and still gain margin. Rules vary by state and must be verified before launch.
first_30_days: Pick one trade (electrical) in one state with clear ratio rules. Recruit 15 retirees from union retiree groups and lapsing-license lists. Sign 5 shops with 3+ helpers who are idle or under-deployed. Bill the first hours in week 3.

title: Trust-Fund Compliance for Family Vloggers
one_liner: A minutes-on-screen tracker and escrow tool that computes, sets aside and documents the trust share owed to kids who appear in monetized family channels.
customer: Family channel operators on YouTube, TikTok and Instagram earning $50k+ a year, influencer agencies and MCNs, and brands and payment processors that want a 'clean hands' certificate.
problem: Several states have passed laws on minors in monetized content: Illinois (2024) requires a trust share by on-screen time, Minnesota (2025) restricts under-14 content creation for pay, and California extended Coogan-style protections (details from memory). Parents compute set-asides by hand. Brands and platforms are exposed, and grown kids and documentaries are fueling backlash.
solution: The tool ingests channel data, uses vision models to measure each child's on-screen minutes per video, computes the state-specific set-aside, generates records and moves funds into a custodial trust, UTMA or custodial investment account. It also keeps consent and deletion logs and issues brand-facing compliance certificates.
why_now: The state laws took effect in 2024-25, public scrutiny of family-vlogging is at a high, and a new custodial-account channel (Trump Accounts, opened July 2026, per the brief) gives set-asides a natural home.
revenue_model: $99-499 a month per channel or about 1% of earnings, plus per-campaign brand compliance certificates.
non_obvious_insight: The real buyers are brands and platforms that need a clean-hands certificate, and creators who need to avoid legal exposure. It works like marketplace sales-tax automation, and the child is the beneficiary, not the customer.
first_30_days: Ship a free on-screen-minutes calculator. DM 100 family channels with 50k-2M subscribers. Sell a $299 compliance setup with an attorney-reviewed template. Approach 3 influencer agencies for a group deal.

title: Repair-Rights Compliance Portal in a Box
one_liner: A hosted repair.yourbrand.com that publishes the parts lists, manuals, pricing and order forms that US state and EU repair laws require, plus the rules engine and audit trail behind it.
customer: Compliance, legal and customer-service leads at mid-market consumer-electronics, appliance, e-bike, power-tool and mobility brands ($30M-$1B revenue) selling in Washington, Texas, Oregon and the EU. Retailers are a second segment.
problem: Washington's law took effect 1 Jan 2026, Texas applies from Sep 2026 to electronics over $50, Oregon bans parts pairing, the EU directive's transposition deadline was 31 Jul 2026, and an EU repair platform is due 1 Jan 2028. Each regime differs in scope, dates and price rules, and the briefing found nobody selling compliance tooling for repair-information forms or parts-availability tracking.
solution: Portal templates and connectors: product-catalog import, SKU mapping to state or EU scope and effective dates, auto-published manuals and parts lists, a parts order form with a fair-price check, pairing-policy disclosures, an SLA timer and request log for regulators, and an EU repair-information-form generator. Regulatory updates ship as configuration changes.
why_now: Multiple obligations hit in the past nine months (Washington Jan 2026, EU transposition Jul 2026, Texas Sep 2026) and Oregon dates are still unclear in public sources, so brands cannot rely on a single law-firm memo.
revenue_model: $15-60k/year per brand by SKU count, $10-30k implementation, and a per-order fee on parts sales.
non_obvious_insight: The core burden of repair law is publication and response time, which is CMS and workflow work, not legal analysis. Law firms bill hourly for what is really a web app, and the portal also cuts support costs.
first_30_days: Pick 30 mid-market brands with Texas exposure from product listings and email compliance leads a free one-page 'Texas gap audit'. Build a minimal portal for three design partners at a $5k pilot fee.

title: File-Cabinet-to-Pipeline Digitization Crew
one_liner: A mobile scan-and-extract crew that turns a newly acquired trades company's filing cabinets and paper job files into a clean customer and equipment-age database plus a ready-to-run replacement and membership campaign.
customer: Acquirers of legacy HVAC, plumbing, roofing, pest, electrical and garage-door companies (search funders, holdcos, PE add-on platforms). The buyer pays a fixed fee plus a share of revenue from jobs sold off the output. Brokers are a secondary channel, using it as sell-side data-room prep.
problem: Acquired trades firms often run on paper, desk phones and old PCs, so the owner cannot see permit errors, warranty problems or job margins. Any AI, field-service software or roll-up integration needs structured data first. Meanwhile decades of installs sit in file drawers as an unused equipment-age database.
solution: A two-person crew with document scanners and phone capture spends 5-10 days on site. Vision-model extraction pulls customer, address, equipment make/model/serial, install date, service history, warranty status and membership status. Output is import-ready for ServiceTitan, Jobber, Housecall Pro and QuickBooks, plus an 'asset-age' list: homes with systems older than a set threshold, expiring warranties, lapsed maintenance customers and contract renewals. It includes a letter/SMS campaign and prepaid-membership offer templates, with job tagging so results are measured.
why_now: Handwriting and form extraction from photos became accurate and cheap in 2025-2026. Bain's 2026 GP outlook says 39% of GPs expect no material financial impact from AI on portfolio companies this year, and Bain's midyear report says leaders redesign workflows rather than layering tools on top. Both point to data readiness as the gap. First-time buyers of small trades firms are more numerous than ever, and each faces the same digitization backlog.
revenue_model: $8-15K fixed fee per business, plus 8-10% of first-year revenue from jobs tagged to campaigns generated from the output. Sell-side version for brokers: $3-5K data-room prep before listing.
non_obvious_insight: What looks like clutter is a proprietary, geocoded equipment-age database of thousands of households, the highest-intent lead list in the trades, and the buyer paid for it in the purchase price without knowing. Rob Brooks found '30,000 customer records' in filing cabinets, 13-year-old computers and desk phones, could not see permit or warranty problems until he digitized, and reached $1.3M EBITDA from $340K SDE in 14 months with about 800 customers prepaying three years of membership (https://www.acquiringminds.co/articles/rob-brooks-gary-air). Winsor Fireform's buyers spent seven months digitizing roughly 90% paper records (https://acquiringminds.co/articles/andrew-sova-alex-clark-winsor-fireform-novo-foundry). Tew & Taylor ran on Excel and mailed checks, creating a large receivables backlog (https://www.acquiringminds.co/articles/jack-rauch-tew-taylor). Bain's GP outlook notes 39% of GPs see no material AI impact on portfolios in 2026 (https://www.bain.com/insights/private-equitys-reality-check-gp-outlook-2026/). Every buyer solved digitization ad hoc, and none treated the archive as revenue.
first_30_days: Pick HVAC in one metro. Find 3 recent small-business buyers through ETA communities and brokers, and offer one a near-cost pilot. Scan and extract 2,000 records in 3 days, mail letters or SMS to the oldest-equipment homes, and count booked calls per 500 contacts. Publish the result as a case study, then price the service at $8-15K plus revenue share. Meanwhile approach 5 HVAC business brokers with the sell-side data-room version.

title: Make Platforms and Receiving Banks Pay Scam Refunds
one_liner: A contingency-fee desk that packages evidence so banks can recover mandatory scam reimbursements from receiving institutions and, in the EU, from the platforms where the scam ran.
customer: UK and EU challenger banks, building societies, credit unions, and e-money and payment institutions. Buyers are fraud-recovery and operations heads.
problem: In the UK, PSPs have had to reimburse authorized push-payment scam victims up to GBP 85K since Oct 2024, with the cost split 50:50 between sending and receiving firms. The EU's provisional PSR deal extends liability to bank-impersonation scams and to platforms that ignore fraud notices. Banks treat reimbursement as a cost of business. Recovering from the other side of the chain (the mule-hosting bank, the ad or profile platform) is manual, slow, and mostly abandoned.
solution: Ingest reimbursed case files and auto-build claim dossiers: a timeline, hash-stamped screenshots of the scam ad or profile, the platform notification and its response time, mule-account indicators, and a funds trace. File claims through scheme channels and formal notices to platforms. Track deadlines and disputes. Get paid a percentage of what is actually recovered.
why_now: Mandatory reimbursement now has more than a year of claim volume in the UK. The EU deal shifts costs toward platforms. Investigations into scam-ad revenue have made platform accountability a political priority. Nobody yet holds the data on which counterparties pay and how fast.
revenue_model: 15-25% contingency on recovered value, with a small SaaS floor. A mid-size UK institution reimbursing GBP 10-30M a year can justify six-figure annual fees.
non_obvious_insight: Liability rules create a claims market. The value chain of counterparties is unbilled because banks were told to reimburse victims, not to chase others, and the recovery data is a compounding moat. Whoever holds it can also sell it to regulators.
first_30_days: Offer 10 UK EMIs and small banks a free audit of 50 reimbursed cases showing recoverable amounts from receiving-side firms and disputed shares. Sign contingency contracts with the first 3. Hire one ex-fraud-ops analyst and use spreadsheets and templates before automating.

title: Router-and-Breaker Screen Control Sold by Trades
one_liner: HVAC, electrical and plumbing shops install tamper-proof, infrastructure-level screen and AI-companion controls as a maintenance-plan add-on for families with kids 8-15.
customer: Home-service shops with 5-30 techs and a maintenance-plan base (they resell the kit), and the parents of 8-15-year-olds who pay $199-349 to install plus $12-18 a month. Slow-season HVAC shops are the first wave.
problem: Under-16 social bans and school phone rules leak: VPNs cost under A$20 a month, seven in ten Australian under-16s reportedly still hold accounts, and only 29% of parents planned full compliance. App-level controls live on the device the kid controls, so they get uninstalled, and they cannot touch consoles, smart TVs, AI toys or AI companion sites. Parents want enforcement kids cannot delete. Meanwhile HVAC shipments fell 25-50% and shops have idle techs and a need for recurring revenue.
solution: A standard 'family network' kit installed in one visit, built from a hardwired or mesh router with router-level policies (VPN and proxy blocking, AI-companion and social categories by age tier, per-device schedules, guest SSID), plus smart-relay outlets ('kid circuits') for consoles and TVs, and a phone-parking charging nook. Parents manage it in a simple app, and shops get a two-hour training course and a quarterly tune-up visit. Cellular data is honestly disclosed as out of scope, and the kit aims at evenings and nights at home.
why_now: Bans and age-assurance rules are live in Australia, Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Texas and Ohio, and Australia is proposing to double fines, so enforcement is the gap. The FTC's 2025 6(b) inquiry and state AI-companion laws put AI chatbots at the center of parental worry. HVAC is at a trough until a 2027 rebound, so shops want add-on services now.
revenue_model: Hardware-plus-install margin split with shops (about $75 spiff plus 30-40% of install), $12-18 per household per month recurring, and training and certification fees for shops.
non_obvious_insight: Software controls sit on the device kids control, so enforcement has to move to infrastructure parents physically own, and installing infrastructure is a trades skill. A local HVAC shop with 2,000 plan customers, most of them families, has near-zero customer acquisition cost compared with consumer parental-control apps.
first_30_days: Build the kit on off-the-shelf router hardware with DNS and VPN filtering and smart relays. Train two local electrical or HVAC shops and pilot 20 installs with a $75 spiff. Log bypass attempts and parent satisfaction, then sign five more shops using the pilot's numbers.

title: Micropollutant Bill Calculator for Generic Drug Makers
one_liner: A dataset and model that estimates each pharma and cosmetics company's share of Europe's new micropollutant treatment bill, sold first to generic manufacturers who cannot pass the cost on.
customer: Generic and OTC drug manufacturers and their trade body, cosmetics makers, and the national producer-responsibility bodies being created to run the scheme. Companies pay subscriptions, and the bodies pay for the allocation licence.
problem: Step one: the revised Urban Wastewater Directive makes pharma and cosmetics makers pay at least 80% of quaternary treatment, with the payment scheme due by end-2028. Cost estimates differ by roughly 10x (EC 1.2B euros, JRC 1.56B, EurEau 3.6-11.2B, Spain alone 24.5B). Step two: each state must allocate cost by load. Step three: generics makers work on thin margins under tender pricing and cannot pass costs through, so they will drop low-margin molecules, causing shortages. Nobody owns the allocation dataset.
solution: A compound-level model of the top 100 active ingredients and cosmetic ingredients: sales volumes from national statistics, excretion and removal rates, ecotoxicity thresholds and plant-upgrade timelines (20% of large plants by 2033, 60% by 2039, 100% by 2045). Output: estimated cost share per marketing-authorisation holder, by state and year, with scenario bands. Compare allocation keys (by mass versus toxicity-weighted).
why_now: Member states are drafting schemes in 2026-2028, and industry lobbying starts now. The 10x cost disagreement means the first credible number will anchor the negotiation.
revenue_model: $30-120k/yr subscriptions per company, $10-20k workshops, and licences to scheme administrators.
non_obvious_insight: The fight is not over whether pharma pays but over how the allocation key is defined, and generics makers and originators want opposite keys. Owning the neutral dataset means owning the terms of the negotiation.
first_30_days: Publish a free 'top 30 molecules' liability preview using public consumption and removal data. Email regulatory-affairs heads at 20 generics makers in Spain, Italy, Poland and India, and at the generics trade body. Sell the first paid workshop for 10-20k euros.

title: Native-Language Translation Earpieces for Dementia Care
one_liner: Dementia-tuned real-time speech translation and a life-story phrasebook so aides can soothe residents in the language they reverted to.
customer: Memory-care communities and nursing homes with multilingual residents, and home-care agencies in NYC, Miami, LA, the Bay Area and Houston.
problem: People with dementia often revert to a first language, while 30% of care workers (60% in New York) are immigrants who speak other languages. The mismatch causes agitation, missed pain, more antipsychotic use and hospital transfers. Compliance-grade phone interpreters are too slow for a 3 am redirect.
solution: An earbud and tablet kit with speech-to-speech translation tuned for dementia (short, slow, warm, repetitive), a preloaded ADL and redirection phrasebook, resident life-story cards in their language (hometown, family, songs), and a video human-interpreter fallback within 30 seconds. Staff dashboards report agitation and PRN antipsychotic use.
why_now: Real-time on-device speech translation reached mainstream earbuds and phones in 2025-26, while visa and TPS shocks are replacing staff with workers who share fewer languages with residents.
revenue_model: $30-60 per resident per month, or $99 per aide per month, plus an implementation fee.
non_obvious_insight: Language access is treated as a compliance checkbox, not a clinical tool. Generic translation isn't tuned to dementia speech and emotion, and the measurable outcome (fewer PRN antipsychotics) is a metric operators already care about.
first_30_days: Identify five memory-care communities with Spanish-, Russian- or Chinese-speaking residents. Run $500 pilots with tablets and an interpreter fallback, and measure PRN antipsychotic use before and after.

title: Persistent Methane Plumes as Equipment Sales Leads
one_liner: Sell satellite-detected methane emitters to the vendors who profit from fixing them: a lead-gen engine, not a compliance tool.
customer: Vapor-recovery-unit makers, flare-gas-to-power microturbine and genset vendors, landfill gas-collection contractors, dairy digester and RNG developers, and small gas gatherers or offtakers. Roughly 2,000 companies in the US; first buyers are sales VPs at 20-person equipment firms.
problem: Abatement vendors prospect blind at trade shows. Emitters are often unaware of a persistent leak or vent, or they do not know its dollar value. A 500 kg/h plume is roughly 230,000 MMBtu a year, or about $0.7M of saleable gas at $3/MMBtu. Methane data today is sold to regulators, ESG buyers and the emitters themselves, and none of them are motivated.
solution: A weekly ranked lead list of persistent emitters, defined as repeated detections across passes from open Carbon Mapper, EMIT and Tanager plume products, with GHGSat tasking to confirm the best leads. Each lead joins the plume to facility ownership (state permits, landfill and EPA datasets), wasted-gas value per year, distance to pipeline or grid, and likely fix type. Delivered as a CRM feed plus a one-page dossier.
why_now: Plume data is now abundant and partly free: Carbon Mapper's Tanager publishes public plume products, and GHGSat is expanding to 16+ satellites. With US federal methane-penalty pressure pushed out, pitches built on fines are weak, while pitches built on recovering saleable gas still work. Cheap gas-to-power gensets and microturbines are also more available.
revenue_model: $2k to $6k a month per vendor per basin or vertical. Success fee of 2% to 4% of first-year equipment or service revenue on closed leads, capped. Later, sell offtake and RNG-interconnect leads to gas buyers.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone treats a methane plume as a violation to be reported. It is really an unmonetized commodity with a known street address and a quantifiable price. Selling the plume to the person who profits from fixing it inverts the market and does not depend on regulation.
first_30_days: Pull open plume data for the Permian, Appalachia and Ohio/Pennsylvania landfills and build the top 100 persistent emitters. Hand-verify ownership and gas value on each. Cold-offer 25 equipment vendors and landfill gas contractors three free leads, then $3k a month. Ask for a paid pilot from 3 by day 30.

title: Stomach-Ready: GLP-1 Protocols for Endoscopy Centers
one_liner: An intake, coaching and point-of-care gastric ultrasound service that stops GLP-1 patients from turning up to endoscopy with a full stomach and getting cancelled on the table.
customer: Independent GI practices and ambulatory surgery centers (ASCs) that run 5-30 endoscopies a day, plus anesthesia groups that staff them. The buyer is the medical director or administrator.
problem: GLP-1 drugs slow gastric emptying. Studies in 2026 show retained gastric contents in roughly one in five endoscopy patients on the drugs, and some procedures are aborted. Guidance has moved from 'stop the drug for a week' to 'continue it, use a 24-hour clear-liquid diet, do selective gastric ultrasound and communicate across teams'. Centers have no operations layer to run this. Front-desk staff cannot tell who is on which drug, at what dose or when the last injection was. Surprises happen day-of, causing cancelled slots, rebooking, extra anesthesia risk and idle rooms.
solution: A text and portal intake flags GLP-1 users (brand, dose, weekly or daily, last injection date, symptoms). It auto-assigns the guideline-based protocol, sends coaching and adjusts dose timing per the clinician's rules. It flags high-risk patients (dose escalation phase, gastroparesis symptoms) for a 90-second gastric POCUS on the day. A travelling RN sonographer or a trained center nurse does the scan with a handheld device, and the result goes straight into the anesthesia record. Phase 2 adds AI-assisted image reading.
why_now: A April 2026 wave of studies (residual gastric content 'far higher than expected') and updated multi-society guidance made continue-and-modify the new standard, which needs new workflows. Oral Wegovy and orforglipron are about to widen the user base. Procedure centers are squeezed on throughput and cannot afford dark rooms.
revenue_model: $15-30 per GLP-1 patient screened and coached, plus $60-100 per gastric ultrasound performed. Alternatively a flat $500-1,500 per site per month. One avoided aborted case is worth roughly $1k+ in recovered slot revenue.
non_obvious_insight: The expensive problem is not the rare aspiration event, it is aborted cases and scheduling chaos. Guidelines supplied a protocol but nobody supplies the operations layer that knows which day of the week each patient injects. The physician societies are a free distribution channel once a protocol is written up.
first_30_days: Get 2-3 GI ASCs on a free 60-day pilot and measure their baseline aborted and rebooked rate. Have a GI and an anesthesiologist advisor sign off on a protocol drawn from published guidance. Build the intake on Twilio and a simple form. Buy two handheld ultrasound units (about $3-5k each) and contract an RN sonographer for spot coverage. Then convert the pilot sites to paid.

title: Documentation-Review Copilot for Notified Bodies and Labs
one_liner: Software that triages and pre-checks manufacturers' technical files for the third-party assessors that CRA, Machinery, radio-cyber and AI Act rules are about to swamp.
customer: EU notified bodies, cybersecurity and Common Criteria test labs and product-certification firms (10-500 staff), including newly designated ones.
problem: Third-party conformity assessment is required for higher-risk classes under several regimes: CRA important-Class II and critical products, the radio-equipment cyber delegated act, new Machinery Regulation duties from 20 Jan 2027, and AI Act biometrics (dates from background knowledge, verify). Assessor capacity is the bottleneck. Each file review takes weeks of expert time on incomplete, inconsistent submissions, and delay lands on the manufacturer's launch date.
solution: An intake portal that bounces incomplete submissions against a clause map, an LLM-assisted cross-check of claims versus test evidence versus SBOM, auto-generated clarification requests to the manufacturer, a reviewer workbench with evidence links, and traceable report drafting. EU-hosted or on-prem for confidentiality.
why_now: CRA reporting began 11 Sep 2026 and further obligations land 11 Dec 2027, while new-body designation and accreditation are slow. File volume is about to rise faster than assessor headcount.
revenue_model: $30-120k/year per lab, or per-reviewer seats at $500-1,500/month, plus implementation fees.
non_obvious_insight: In any permit regime the scarce resource is the assessor's hours, and manufacturers pay for delay. Selling to roughly 150 known assessors is easier than selling to 100,000 manufacturers, and it produces unique data on what a 'good file' looks like.
first_30_days: Email 40 labs and notified bodies and offer to pilot on a backlog of anonymized historical files. Run three paid pilots at EUR 5-10k, measure review-hours saved, and turn the results into a case study.

title: Battery-Buffered Induction Kitchens for LPG-Starved Restaurants
one_liner: A load-sharing controller and optional battery lets Indian cloud kitchens and restaurants switch from scarce LPG to induction without waiting months for a utility load upgrade, then pools the fleet as a lunch-and-dinner-peak resource for DISCOMs.
customer: Cloud kitchens, small restaurant chains (5-50 outlets), hostel and office messes, caterers and sweet shops in Indian metros and tier-2 cities.
problem: The Hormuz-driven LPG shortage pushed induction cooktop demand up 20-25x and the government is distributing 500k stoves, but a commercial kitchen converting needs roughly 15-40 kW of extra connected load. DISCOM sanctioned-load upgrades and neighborhood transformers are slow and constrained, and the switch could add up to 27 GW of national demand at the evening peak. Low-income uptake is reported as sluggish because grid and financing are not ready.
solution: A CT-clamp controller (about $300-400) that sequences burners so total draw stays under the sanctioned load, since cooking tolerates duty-cycling. Add a 20-60 kWh LFP buffer to cover lunch and dinner peaks, financed as a monthly cooking-energy subscription through an NBFC and charged off-peak or on midday solar. The aggregated fleet later sells peak flexibility to DISCOMs under state demand-side management programs.
why_now: LPG scarcity is forcing commercial conversion now, stationary LFP packs are around $70/kWh, smart-meter and demand-side management programs are rolling out, and utilities cannot build capacity fast enough (transformer lead times, capex-biased regulation).
revenue_model: Controller sale of INR 25-35k, battery lease or subscription of roughly INR 15-30k per month (benchmarked against the commercial LPG bill it replaces, when LPG is available at all), and later DISCOM peak-flex payments per kW-year plus midday-charging arbitrage.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck to electrifying cooking is not the stove but the permission to draw power at the kitchen's meter. A battery and a scheduler turn an infrastructure-approval problem into a financing problem. Cooking is a rare thermal load that can be shaped without harming the product, so the cheap controller does most of the work and generates the data that later sells flexibility.
first_30_days: Sell 10 controllers to cloud kitchens in one metro through restaurant associations and cloud-kitchen operator WhatsApp groups. Log load data and outages, then lease batteries to the first 3 with an NBFC partner. Use the aggregated load data to open a sandbox conversation with one DISCOM.

title: Blended-Beef Extender for Grinders and Schools
one_liner: Sell a fiber-and-protein extender that stretches ground beef 20-30% and adds fiber, instead of trying to replace beef.
customer: Regional ground-beef grinders, further processors, and school and institutional foodservice distributors.
problem: Retail beef hit a record $9.64/lb with the smallest herd in 75 years, and Mexican feeder cattle are halted. Plant-based meat failed as a replacement, so buyers have no cost-relief tool.
solution: A mushroom, legume and oat fiber-protein blend with a clean label, tested in 70/30 and 80/20 beef blends, sold by the ton with USDA-compliant blended-product labeling and recipe support.
why_now: Record beef prices, screwworm-driven supply risk, and GLP-1 users who want more protein and fiber per bite make a cheaper high-fiber blended patty newly attractive.
revenue_model: Ingredient sales per pound, co-development fees, and multi-year supply agreements with distributors.
non_obvious_insight: Plant-based meat lost as an identity swap but wins as a cost and fiber additive inside real beef, where the buyer never has to change what they say they are selling.
first_30_days: Contract a food-science lab to build three blends, send samples to about 10 regional grinders and two school-food distributors, and start FSIS labeling work.

title: Human-Review Receipts for the EU Text Exemption
one_liner: Sell signed proof that a named human reviewed and took responsibility for AI-assisted text, which is the thing the EU's disclosure rule for text appears to reward, not labels on AI.
customer: Newsletter operators, niche and local publishers, and B2B content agencies that publish AI-assisted text to EU readers. Second buyers are legal and compliance leads at mid-market publishers.
problem: The industry reads EU AI Act Art. 50 (applicable Aug 2, 2026) as 'label the AI.' My understanding of Art. 50(4) is that the text-disclosure duty for public-interest publications has an exemption where content underwent human review or editorial control and a person holds editorial responsibility. Confirm the exact wording with counsel, because the brief does not quote it. Meanwhile readers get accusation tools: Substack embedded Pangram scanning on Jul 22 and LinkedIn added a slop-report button on Jul 30. Publishers have no defensible record of human review.
solution: A Ghost, WordPress and Substack-compatible plugin plus API that records, per article, the AI draft versus the final diff, who reviewed it, and a passkey-signed approval bound to the content hash. It publishes a verification page and a byline element ('reviewed and edited by [name]'), and generates an evidence binder for regulators and clients. If no review is recorded, it falls back to an automatic disclosure line.
why_now: Art. 50 became applicable on Aug 2, 2026, and reader-side detection has just been built into major platforms. The first regulatory questions and client audits will land on publishers this year.
revenue_model: $29-99/month per publication, $500-2,000/month agency plans, and $250 per audit-ready evidence binder.
non_obvious_insight: Detection tries to prove a negative ('not AI'). The law's structure turns human review into a legal safe harbor, so the sellable product is a positive: a named person accepted responsibility. That gives 'human-made' a compliance budget instead of an ethics budget.
first_30_days: Ship a Ghost/WordPress plugin with diff capture and passkey sign-off in about three weeks. Approach 10 EU-facing newsletters and 3 agencies with 'Aug 2 has passed, where is your evidence?' Co-brand the evidence binder with one EU tech-law boutique that can use it as a channel.

title: Rain-Day Revenue Insurance for Patio Restaurants
one_liner: Parametric weather cover for restaurants: pick your bad-weather trigger, get paid automatically when it hits, with payouts calibrated to your own POS history.
customer: Independent restaurants and bars with 1-10 units and meaningful patio or walk-up dependence, starting in weather-volatile metros (rain, extreme heat, wildfire smoke). The owner pays a seasonal premium of roughly $40-150 per location per month. A licensed MGA/carrier partner and reinsurer sit behind the product.
problem: A rainy Friday, a 105F heat-index evening or a smoke day (AQI over 150) can cut a patio-dependent night by 30-50%. The food is already prepped and the staff are already scheduled, so almost all of the lost revenue is lost margin. Business-interruption insurance needs physical damage, so weather-driven demand loss is uninsured. Every owner knows their 'rain tax' (I know a wet Saturday costs me several thousand dollars), yet no one sells a hedge for it.
solution: Owners connect Toast, Square or Clover, and we ingest 12-24 months of hourly sales. We fit each location's loss curve against local weather-station history, for example rain over 0.15 in between 5 and 9pm Fri-Sun, or heat index above 105. The owner picks triggers and a fixed payout per trigger day. When the station data crosses the threshold, the payout goes out automatically by instant rails, with no claim and no adjuster. Because triggers are calibrated per restaurant, basis risk is low, which is what has kept carriers away from this segment. We sell it as a seasonal policy with a monthly premium.
why_now: POS APIs now give clean hourly sales for thousands of independents in minutes. Weather-station and air-quality data are cheap and auditable. Instant payment rails (FedNow, RTP) exist. Heat domes and smoke seasons are making weather volatility a top-3 owner complaint. Reinsurers are hungry for parametric programs, and restaurants face rising conventional premiums that push them to look for smarter cover. I could not re-verify current competitors this session, so check the existing parametric MGAs and event-cancellation carriers before building.
revenue_model: MGA commission plus underwriting margin on premium, typically 15-30% of premium retained as fee and MGA share. Roughly $500-1,800 per location per year in premium. Add a fee for the POS-calibrated loss-curve analytics, sold to carriers and reinsurers as a data product.
non_obvious_insight: The trick is that the owner's POS data, not a claims adjuster, is the underwriting. Basis risk is what kills parametric for small businesses, and a restaurant's own hourly sales history fixes it. Insurers think restaurants are too heterogeneous to price. They are only heterogeneous until you fit each one separately. The loss is also asymmetric: prepped food and committed labor mean a payout only has to cover the lost contribution margin, not the revenue, so premiums can be low.
first_30_days: Use my two locations' POS exports plus 10 friendly patio owners' data to fit loss curves and prove the weather-to-sales correlation. Publish a free 'Rain Tax Report' for one metro to generate leads. Sign a licensed MGA or fronting-carrier partner. Collect 10-15 signed letters of intent at about $60 per month for the next patio season. Since it is late September, use the off-season to finish modeling and pre-sell spring renewals.

title: Rare Blood Group Assay Foundry
one_liner: Turn each newly recognized blood-group gene into research-use genotyping controls and panels for reference labs, starting with the MAL deletions that define AnWj-negative blood.
customer: Immunohematology reference labs, rare-donor programs and blood centers. Blood-group genotyping platform vendors that want to add content are a second buyer.
problem: AnWj-negative patients, over 99.9% of people are AnWj-positive, can form antibodies against AnWj and risk serious transfusion reactions from ordinary units, and compatible donors are 'extraordinarily difficult' to find. Antibody testing finds the patients but cannot identify rare genetic carriers or donors. Volumes are too small for large diagnostics companies to prioritize.
solution: A small molecular-biology team designs, validates and sells RUO kits: synthetic positive-control DNA for the published MAL deletions, primer and probe sets, and a small validation panel. It then repeats the process for each new ISBT system or rare antigen as the genes are published. It also licenses content to genotyping platform vendors and offers a sample-testing service for rare-donor registries.
why_now: MAL was formally recognized as ISBT blood group system 047 in 2026, and the authors say genotyping tests 'can potentially be incorporated into existing blood group genotyping systems.' Nobody has yet turned the finding into a commercial assay. Cheap gene synthesis and long-read or targeted sequencing make a low-volume, high-value control kit practical for a small team.
revenue_model: RUO control and primer kits at roughly $500-2,000 each, per-sample testing fees for registries, and content-licensing or royalty deals with platform vendors. Later, a CLIA or LDT lab service.
non_obvious_insight: Every new blood-group gene discovery creates a diagnostic gap that big vendors ignore because volume is tiny, and the 47th ISBT system was only just recognized. The NHS Blood and Transplant discovery took nearly 20 years and states that serological testing 'cannot identify rare genetic cases without genetic sequencing' (https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/09/260918024828.htm; Blood 2024, DOI 10.1182/blood.2024025099). A repeatable foundry that converts each new ISBT gene into a control kit captures a stream of these gaps. Rare-donor matching is a high-willingness-to-pay niche because a single unmatched patient can cost a hospital far more than a kit.
first_30_days: Design gBlock-style synthetic controls for the MAL deletion alleles reported in the Blood paper and validate them on public or donated DNA. Contact the NHS Blood and Transplant IBGRL, the American Rare Donor Program and 5-10 US and EU reference labs to trial the RUO kit. Line up a second gene from the recent ISBT additions. Pitch two platform vendors on a content deal.

title: Group-Block Attrition and Force Majeure Claims Desk
one_liner: A 48-hour, outcome-priced desk that tells meeting and wedding planners whether the 2026 shocks let them escape or shrink hotel attrition penalties, and files the notices on time.
customer: Association and corporate meeting planners without in-house counsel (100-1,000 attendees), destination-wedding planners, DMCs, and youth-sports or choir tour operators holding hotel room blocks.
problem: Hormuz closure (2 Mar 2026), jet-fuel-driven capacity cuts and fare hikes, and UAE hospitality disruption mean groups cannot fill contracted blocks, while booking lead times shrank from 37.5 to 33 days. Attrition clauses often penalize around 20% shortfalls, and force-majeure wording and notice deadlines, not the law, decide outcomes. Small planners miss the 7-30 day notice windows and pay in full.
solution: Upload the contract for a clause map covering the attrition table, cure and mitigation duties, force-majeure triggers, and deadlines. The desk generates the notice letters, sends deadline alerts, and provides a negotiation script and a walk-away vs renegotiate calculator. A partner hospitality lawyer handles escalations at a fixed fee. Cases where the hotel resold freed rooms at higher rates argue mitigation, not force majeure.
why_now: The 2026 disruption produced a wave of disputes between now and winter events. Europe summer ADR rose 4-6% and Turkey flights rose 25% as trips rerouted. In those markets hotels can resell freed blocks at higher prices, which weakens their damages claims.
revenue_model: $390 flat for the clause map and deadline pack, about 15% of penalties avoided as a success fee, and fixed-fee lawyer escalations. An annual $1,200 deadline-tracker subscription is aimed at DMCs.
non_obvious_insight: The strongest argument is often mitigation, not force majeure. In rerouting hot spots the hotel resells rooms at higher rates and cannot claim losses it did not suffer. The moat is a dataset of clause wording and outcomes, plus never missing a deadline.
first_30_days: Recruit 20 planners from association-executive and wedding-planner forums with a free 'contract triage' of one block. Have one hospitality lawyer review the template letters. Convert the first 5 to paid flat-fee packs and log every outcome to build the clause database.

title: Error-Rate Cliff Insurance for SNAP Agencies
one_liner: A managed QC service that re-reads a sample of newly approved and recertified SNAP cases against federal review rules and builds federal-dispute packets, sold to county and state agencies facing cost-share penalties.
customer: County social-services directors in county-administered states (NC, CO, MN, NY, OH, VA and others), state QC units, and state agencies with error rates at or above 6%. In FY2025, 20 states were at 10% or higher.
problem: Illinois's FY2025 SNAP error rate was 14.7%. Its DHS estimates roughly $700M of penalty exposure, is hiring 450 staff for $55M, and faces admin costs rising from $60M to $100M as the state share of SNAP admin costs goes from 50% to 75% in October 2026. In North Carolina, Wilson County's DSS (about $13M budget) faces up to $4.2M in penalties with no state relief, and the state's eligibility system (NC FAST) has no document portal or AI. Counties report ~10% vacancy and staff with about a year of experience. Illinois DHS says most errors are 'minor errors', and the federal definition of an error is any variance of $57 or more.
solution: Each week, supervisors upload a 5-10% sample of case files per caseworker. AI extracts income, household composition, deductions and verification documents, recomputes the benefit under federal and state policy, and flags variances of $57 or more with the policy citation. Supervisors get a fix-before-QC list. For cases in the federal QC sample, the tool builds the dispute or arbitration packet comparing the state review with the federal findings. Certified ex-state QC reviewers sign off on anything high-stakes. Deploy inside the county's own cloud tenant so no PII leaves.
why_now: H.R. 1 shifts benefit-cost sharing to states by error-rate tier, with the top tier at 15% of benefit costs for rates of 10% or more. Penalties begin in FY2028-29, starting October 2027 per Capitol News Illinois. The admin-cost shift hits October 2026. Agencies are also absorbing Medicaid work-requirement workloads, so they cannot hire their way to accuracy.
revenue_model: Per-case-reviewed fee ($15-40 range to test) or annual county subscription of $40-150k. For comparison, one county eligibility worker costs $40-95k a year. Optional shared-savings pricing tied to avoided penalty tier.
non_obvious_insight: The penalty is a cliff function by error-rate band, so fixing a handful of cases near a threshold can be worth millions, which makes a cheap second-look service priced like insurance. In county-administered states, each of ~100 counties (NC) is a separate small buyer that carries its own penalty exposure. The cost of the problem is in the evidence: Illinois's 14.7% rate, ~$700M exposure, 450 hires and $55M budget (https://capitolnewsillinois.com/news/illinois-food-assistance-error-rate-continues-to-grow-as-federal-penalties-loom/). NC's 10% vacancy, Wilson County's $4.2M penalty exposure on a $13M budget, and staff with 11-13 months' experience (https://www.northcarolinahealthnews.org/2026/04/30/medicaid-work-county-challenges/). Job-posting signal: governmentjobs.com showed about 2,000 'eligibility worker' results on 2026-09-28 at roughly $40-95k salaries (https://www.governmentjobs.com/jobs?keyword=eligibility%20worker). Indiana is hiring 400 people to check eligibility (https://indianacapitalchronicle.com/2026/04/29/fssa-hiring-400-medicaid-eligibility-checkers-ahead-of-work-requirements/) and Pennsylvania has about 400 open county positions (https://kffhealthnews.org/medicaid/medicaid-cuts-work-requirements-state-staff-shortages/). Caveat: the tier percentages and FY start dates come from the article and my recollection of the law and should be re-verified.
first_30_days: Target North Carolina, where about 100 counties buy independently in small increments. Recruit 2 retired state QC reviewers as advisers. Offer 3 county DSS directors a free retrospective audit of 100 closed cases, showing errors the county's own review missed. Convert to a paid pilot under the county's small-purchase threshold. Confirm security requirements (in-tenant deployment, redaction) before touching real case files.

title: Pre-Confirmation Screwworm Risk Feed for Cattle Markets
one_liner: A county-level early-warning feed that fuses news, vet reports, weather and zone announcements to give cattle buyers, auction barns and insurers days or weeks of lead time over official lab confirmation.
customer: Auction markets and sale barns, feedlots and stocker buyers, livestock lenders and insurers, and cattle-futures or ag-commodity desks. Ranchers and vet clinics are a low-price tier.
problem: New World screwworm has reached Texas and New Mexico. The UC San Diego team building a tracker says official reporting lags: 'Lab confirmation can take days or weeks.' Cattle prices, hauling rules and purchase decisions move on rumor and news before confirmation. Producers have no single source for zone status and their own exposure.
solution: A subscription feed that scores county-level risk from public and semi-public signals: state and APHIS zone announcements, extension and vet-clinic posts, local news, trap and case reports, and fly-friendly temperature and humidity. It sends SMS or email alerts and a plain-language 'movement readiness' checklist for each zone. Users can submit their own sightings, which improves the model. Sold in tiers from a $99/month producer plan to trading-desk contracts.
why_now: The screwworm reached the US Southwest in 2026, and APHIS newsroom items on 18 and 21 September 2026 show Texas releasing infested zones. The academic dashboard is a research tool, not a commercial product, and the sterile-fly response is slow to scale, so risk and compliance uncertainty will last through at least one fly season.
revenue_model: Producer and barn subscriptions at $99-500/month, insurer, lender and buyer contracts at $2-10k/month, and enterprise API fees for commodity desks.
non_obvious_insight: The academic value of the dashboard is the reporting lag itself: the UC San Diego team added media reports because 'lab confirmation can take days or weeks' (https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/09/260914102439.htm). The paying customer is anyone whose money moves on news before USDA confirms, meaning buyers, hedgers and insurers, not the county health officials the tool was built for. The lag is the product. Recent APHIS announcements show zone status is changing week to week (https://www.aphis.usda.gov/news).
first_30_days: Build a scraper and manual-curation pipeline over APHIS and Texas Animal Health Commission announcements, extension and vet feeds, and local news, plus a weather-based fly-activity index. Publish a free weekly map to gather emails. Pitch 10 sale barns and 3 commodity or insurer desks a paid pilot and sell the first 5 at a founding discount. Contact the UC San Diego team about a data and methods collaboration. Note that the APHIS screwworm page consulted in this session still said the pest was absent from the US, so confirm current case status before launch.

title: Alcohol Bridge: GLP-1 Addiction Care for Hospitals
one_liner: A hospital-embedded service that starts naltrexone plus semaglutide at discharge for alcohol use disorder with PEth monitoring.
customer: Hospital addiction-consult teams and liver clinics, plus health plans and employers paying for alcohol-related admissions.
problem: Only ~2% of people with alcohol use disorder get medication. A Lancet RCT (May 2026, n=108) showed semaglutide cut heavy drinking days in AUD with obesity, with NNT ~4.3 vs 7+ for approved drugs, and NIH-reported work shows added benefit on top of CBT. Phase 3 trials and the VA's CRAVE trial are running, but clinicians have no protocol, and opioid bridge clinics got settlement money while alcohol, the bigger killer, got none.
solution: A bridge service at discharge: naltrexone alone or with semaglutide (per trial eligibility, BMI 30 or more), PEth blood monitoring every 4 weeks, telehealth follow-ups and a cash-pay pill pathway, with outcome reporting on readmissions and PEth negatives.
why_now: The first RCT and NIH coverage landed in 2026, GLP-1s are now cheap and familiar, and hospitals are under margin pressure from readmissions. Off-label use requires careful protocols, so first movers will set the standard.
revenue_model: $250-400 per patient per month billed to hospitals, payers or employers, plus grant and state SUD funds where eligible.
non_obvious_insight: Alcohol-related admissions repeat and cost the hospital, but no service line owns the medication step. The wedge is a discharge protocol, not a new clinic.
first_30_days: Approach 3 hospital addiction-consult teams and hepatology clinics. Recruit an addiction-boarded medical director and run a 30-patient quality-improvement pilot under the hospital's existing governance, charging a ~$20k pilot fee.

title: Pooled Tariff-Surcharge Refund Claims for Small Buyers
one_liner: Connect to small businesses' accounting data, find tariff surcharges they paid distributors, and pool their claims against the same suppliers now receiving IEEPA refunds.
customer: Restaurants and restaurant groups, contractors, small manufacturers and retailers that bought through distributors who added tariff surcharge lines in 2025, paying on contingency.
problem: The Supreme Court struck down the IEEPA tariffs in February 2026, and CBP began taking refund claims through its CAPE portal on April 20, 2026, with roughly $175B owed to about 330,000 importers. Suppliers who passed the tariff through on itemized surcharges are now collecting refunds. Small buyers who paid those lines have claims but no visibility and no lawyer, since a $3k claim is uneconomic to pursue alone.
solution: Read 24 months of AP data (QuickBooks, Bill.com, email invoices) with an LLM to isolate itemized surcharges and post-tariff price jumps by supplier. Aggregate each supplier's small-buyer claims into one pooled demand or arbitration or class action through a partner consumer-protection firm. Track which suppliers have filed for refunds. Later, add econometric analysis of 'embedded' non-itemized price increases.
why_now: Refunds are being issued now (typically 60 to 90 days after acceptance), so the window for suppliers to hold and spend the money is short. Pass-through disputes have begun to appear in courts, but law firms focus on large B2B claimants. Litigation and CBP timing remains uncertain (the government appealed the refund order), which favors moving fast.
revenue_model: 20% to 30% contingency on recovered amounts, plus a fixed fee to run the AP analysis for larger buyers.
non_obvious_insight: Claims are tiny individually but concentrated by supplier. Two hundred restaurants that all bought from the same three distributors are a multimillion-dollar claim against three defendants. The supplier-level dataset (who added surcharges, when, how much, who filed) is the moat, and it is built one small customer at a time.
first_30_days: Build a free 'surcharge finder' that scans an uploaded invoice export or QuickBooks connection and shows what was paid. Recruit through restaurant and contractor associations and bookkeepers. Sign 50 claimants on contingency and target the 10 distributors whose surcharges show up most often. Line up a partner litigation firm.

title: Universal Viva: AI-Run Oral Verification
one_liner: After each major submission the student takes a five-minute identity-verified voice conversation with an AI examiner about their own work, and humans review only the flagged mismatches.
customer: Online and community-college programs, university departments, dual-enrollment providers and credentialing bootcamps (department chairs and deans), later honor councils.
problem: At Harvard 89% of professors received suspected AI work but only 12% referred cases, and 67% say AI hurts their courses. Detectors are unreliable and biased against non-native writers (lower-confidence data). Oral exams work but do not scale: 300 students at 15 minutes each is 75 hours.
solution: A voice agent reads the submission, asks 6-8 adaptive questions on reasoning, sources and choices, checks consistency with the submitted work, and returns a comprehension score. Low-scoring cases go to a bench of trained human examiners. It measures whether the student understands the work rather than accusing anyone of using AI, with accommodations for disabilities and language.
why_now: Real-time voice models with natural turn-taking and low latency matured in 2025-26. Faculty sentiment has turned sharply negative and detection has failed, so institutions need a fairer alternative before the next term's grades.
revenue_model: $3-6 per verification paid by the institution or $30 per student per course, with premium pricing for human audit and site licenses.
non_obvious_insight: Detection asks 'did an AI write this?', which is unanswerable and adversarial. Verification asks 'does the student understand this?', which is answerable, fairer to non-native writers, and much harder to outsource live in a voice conversation.
first_30_days: Pilot with 3 professors in writing-intensive intro courses at a community college, about 60 students. Compare oral-comprehension scores with graded essays and show an instructor dashboard. Move to $4 per verification after the pilot. Set voice-data retention and accessibility policies before launch.
